linux.fallback: IPv4 ARP entries only; /proc/net/arp carries no IPv6 neighbours (they live in the RTM_GETNEIGH table), and non-Ethernet or incomplete entries are not reported

macos.fallback: ip and mac only; the interface name and static/dynamic type are not carried by the RTF_LLINFO dump and are emitted as '-'

linux.fallback: falls back to systemd-resolve statistics, or reports unavailable, when resolvectl is absent
reads the *_proxy variables from the agent process's own environment only; a system-wide, desktop-session or package-manager proxy the agent did not inherit is not reported

macos.fallback: reports the HTTP proxy and PAC URL, checking the primary network service first and then each scoped per-interface service; HTTPS/SOCKS/FTP proxies are not reported, so a host configured with only those reads as none

linux.fallback: main and custom routing tables, IPv4 and IPv6; the local table, cloned entries and host-local route types are not reported; a multipath route reports its first nexthop only and an `ip nexthop` object route carries no resolved gateway (both flagged in the result status)

macos.fallback: IPv4 and IPv6; macOS has no route metric or table id, so those fields are '-', and the origin is only the RTF_STATIC bit (static, which also covers connected-interface routes), else RTF_DYNAMIC/RTF_MODIFIED (dynamic), else other; entries flagged as neighbour (RTF_LLINFO), cloned, multicast, broadcast or own-address (RTF_LOCAL) are not reported (the limited-broadcast 255.255.255.255/32 route carries none of those flags and is); interface-scoped routes (RTF_IFSCOPE) are listed like any other

windows.fallback: IPv4 and IPv6; the host's own and broadcast addresses (Protocol Local, full-length prefix) and the multicast prefixes are not reported, connected-subnet routes are; the metric is the route metric alone, without the interface metric

caveats: **Windows `speed_mbps` is not clamped for an unknown-speed adapter.** `TransmitLinkSpeed` is divided by 1,000,000 with no sentinel check (`do_adapters`); when the API reports its "unknown speed" value (`ULONG64_MAX`) the row shows `18446744073709` instead of `0`, as on three of the nine adapters in the Windows sample (`WiFi`, `Local Area Connection* 1`, `Local Area Connection* 2`). Any consumer treating `speed_mbps` as a real figure must guard against that value.

**Each action sees less than its name suggests.** On Windows `adapters`, `ip_addresses` and `dns_servers` skip loopback and tunnel-type adapters (other VPN adapter types, such as the Tailscale adapter in the sample, are listed), and `proxy` returns the agent account's settings, not a signed-in user's. On Linux `dns_servers` reads only `/etc/resolv.conf` and `proxy` only the agent's inherited environment, so a resolver or proxy managed elsewhere is not reported.

**Some row shapes differ by platform and are not normalised.** `dns_cache` has no shared shape (a structured `name|type|0|` row on Windows, one raw line under `cache_entry|` or a `dns_stats|` line on Linux, an `unsupported` row on macOS), so a consumer that parses `cache_entry|` as name, type and TTL everywhere will misparse Linux. Linux `proxy_type` is the raw environment-variable name (`http_proxy`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, ...) and can appear several times in one response, where Windows and macOS emit `none`, `http`, `pac` or `auto_detect` once. `ip_addresses.gateway` is per adapter on Windows but one host-wide value repeated on every row on macOS and Linux.

**The `adapters` loopback asymmetry is deliberate; do not "align" it.** Linux leaves out `lo`, while macOS reports `lo0` as a real adapter. Changing either side silently alters what the fleet reports.

**`routes` is the configured table, filtered differently on each OS.** Linux reports the main and custom tables but drops the local table, cloned entries and local, broadcast, anycast and multicast route types, shows only the first nexthop of a multipath route, and shows an `ip nexthop`-object route's gateway as `nhid:<n>` (the last two are flagged in the result status). macOS has no metric or table id (both `-`), calls a route `static` whenever the kernel sets `RTF_STATIC` (which includes connected-interface routes that Linux calls `kernel` and Windows `local`), lists interface-scoped routes like any other, and drops the entries the kernel flags as neighbour, cloned, multicast, broadcast or own-address (the filter is flag-based, so an ordinary host route such as `255.255.255.255/32` can still appear). Windows reports the route metric alone (the interface metric Windows adds when ranking routes is not shown) and drops the host's own, broadcast and multicast prefixes while keeping connected-subnet routes, so a cross-OS comparison must not assume the same filter or the same `origin` vocabulary.

definitions.description: Lists network adapters with MAC address, link speed, and operational status. On Windows uses GetAdaptersAddresses and skips loopback and tunnel interfaces; on Linux reads rtnetlink (RTM_GETLINK) plus sysfs speed and skips loopback; on macOS reads getifaddrs and SIOCGIFMEDIA and reports loopback (lo0) as a real adapter. The loopback difference between Linux and macOS is long-standing behaviour, not an oversight. On Linux the adapter name is the kernel interface name, so devices with a parent link (veth, VLAN, tunnel) are reported as eth0 rather than iproute2's display form eth0@if74.

Returns the host ARP / neighbour table (interface, IP, MAC address, static/dynamic type). On Windows reads GetIpNetTable2 — IPv4 ARP and IPv6 neighbours, including incomplete entries, capped at 20000 rows. On Linux reads /proc/net/arp: IPv4 ARP only — IPv6 neighbours live in a separate kernel table and are not reported, and non-Ethernet or incomplete (non-ATF_COM) entries are skipped. On macOS reads a PF_ROUTE RTF_LLINFO sysctl and de-duplicates; the dump carries no interface name or static/dynamic type, so both fields are reported as "-". Linux and macOS share Windows' 20000-row cap. This collects the host's known neighbour identities (IP + MAC address) and is tagged for compliance/inventory review on that basis.

Dumps the local DNS resolver cache. On Windows dynamically loads DnsGetCacheDataTable from dnsapi.dll and returns cached entries with record type (A, AAAA, CNAME, PTR, MX, SRV). On Linux reads resolvectl cache or falls back to systemd-resolve statistics. On macOS the OS does not expose resolver-cache contents to userspace (dscacheutil -cachedump is defunct on modern macOS), so a single dns_cache|unsupported sentinel is returned — a permanent capability gap, not a transient failure.

Lists configured DNS servers per adapter, including address family (IPv4/IPv6). On Windows enumerates per-adapter DNS server addresses via GetAdaptersAddresses. On Linux reads /etc/resolv.conf nameserver entries. On macOS reads SCDynamicStore, unioning the global resolver key with every per-service resolver key so supplemental (VPN split-DNS, secondary-interface) resolvers are included, de-duplicated in first-seen order.

Lists assigned IP addresses per adapter with subnet prefix length and default gateway. Returns both IPv4 and IPv6 unicast addresses. On Windows uses GetAdaptersAddresses with GAA_FLAG_INCLUDE_GATEWAYS, on Linux reads rtnetlink (RTM_GETADDR/RTM_GETROUTE), on macOS reads getifaddrs plus a PF_ROUTE sysctl for the default route. Loopback is excluded on Linux and macOS. The Linux default gateway is taken from the main routing table only, matching ip route show default; policy-routing tables installed by VPNs are ignored.

Returns the system proxy configuration including proxy type, proxy address, and bypass list. On Windows reads WinHTTP IE proxy config and reports a normalized proxy_type (none, http, pac, auto_detect). On Linux checks the http_proxy/HTTP_PROXY/https_proxy/HTTPS_PROXY/all_proxy/ ALL_PROXY/no_proxy/NO_PROXY environment variables and reports the LITERAL variable name as proxy_type (not a normalized type), emitting one proxy_type/proxy_address row pair per variable that is set. On macOS reads SCDynamicStoreCopyProxies, checking the primary network service first and then each scoped per-interface service, so a proxy configured on a service that is not currently active is still reported; only the HTTP proxy and PAC URL are reported, so a host configured with only an HTTPS, SOCKS or FTP proxy reads as none. macOS and Linux (no_proxy) also emit a bypass row listing the proxy exception list.

Returns the host routing table, IPv4 and IPv6 together: destination prefix, gateway, interface, metric, table, type and origin, capped at 20000 rows. On Linux reads one rtnetlink RTM_GETROUTE dump covering the main table and any custom table (VPN and policy routing live there), including blackhole, unreachable, prohibit and throw routes; the local table, cloned entries and host-local route types are not reported, a multipath route reports its first nexthop only and an "ip nexthop" object route carries no resolved gateway (both flagged in the result status). On macOS reads the PF_ROUTE NET_RT_DUMP sysctl for every address family; macOS has no route metric or table id, so those are "-", and the origin is only the static bit (which also covers connected-interface routes), else the dynamic or redirect-modified bit; entries flagged as neighbour, cloned, multicast, broadcast or own-address are not reported (the limited-broadcast 255.255.255.255/32 route carries none of those flags and is), and interface-scoped routes (one default per VPN tunnel, say) are listed like any other. On Windows reads GetIpForwardTable2; the metric is the route metric alone, without the interface metric Windows adds when ranking routes, and the host's own and broadcast addresses and the multicast prefixes are not reported. A route table that cannot be read at all is reported as unavailable, never as an empty table.

description: Reports network adapter configuration, IP addresses, DNS servers, proxy settings, and the routing table
how_it_works:
The plugin reports how a device is attached to its network: its adapters, addresses, resolvers, proxy, resolver cache, neighbour (ARP) table and routing table. Every action is one local read with no state, no network traffic and no background collection; the definitions' `gather.ttlSeconds` (30 to 120 seconds) is the time the agent has to answer, not a cache. Each OS answers through its own native interface rather than by parsing command output, with one exception: the Linux resolver cache runs `resolvectl`. Nothing here captures packets or tests connectivity: the plugin says what the host is configured to do, not what the network does.

| Action | Windows | macOS | Linux |
|---|---|---|---|
| `adapters` | `GetAdaptersAddresses`; loopback and tunnel-type adapters are left out | `getifaddrs` and `SIOCGIFMEDIA`; `lo0` is listed | rtnetlink link dump; `lo` is left out |
| `ip_addresses` | `GetAdaptersAddresses`; each adapter's own first gateway | `getifaddrs` plus the routing-socket default route; one host-wide gateway | rtnetlink address and route dump; one host-wide default gateway |
| `dns_servers` | each adapter's DNS list | SystemConfiguration dynamic store | `nameserver` lines of `/etc/resolv.conf` |
| `proxy` | WinHTTP Internet Explorer settings of the agent account | SystemConfiguration proxy settings (HTTP and PAC only) | `*_proxy` variables in the agent's own environment |
| `dns_cache` | `DnsGetCacheDataTable` | not supported (returns an `unsupported` row) | `resolvectl cache`, else `systemd-resolve --statistics` |
| `arp` | `GetIpNetTable2` | routing-socket neighbour dump | `/proc/net/arp` (IPv4 only) |
| `routes` | `GetIpForwardTable2` | routing-socket `NET_RT_DUMP` | rtnetlink `RTM_GETROUTE` for IPv4 and IPv6 |

`arp` and `routes` each stop at 20,000 rows so a very large or forged table cannot grow a response without bound. `routes` reports the configured table (IPv4 and IPv6 together, with destination prefix, gateway, interface, metric, table, route type and origin), not the host's own addresses, and only after per-OS filtering described under Caveat 5. A read that fails or is cut short is reported through the result status, never as an empty success.

### What you can decide with it

| Question | Action | How to read it, and what it cannot tell you |
|---|---|---|
| Is this device sending all its traffic through a VPN? | `routes` | Look at the default routes (`prefix_len` 0, destination `0.0.0.0` or `::`) and at the split-default pair `0.0.0.0/1` and `128.0.0.0/1` (IPv6 `::/1` and `8000::/1`) that many VPN clients install. A default or split-default route whose `interface` is the VPN adapter means a full tunnel; routes for specific networks via the VPN with a different default means a split tunnel. The table lists routes, it does not work out which route wins for a destination, and on Linux the policy rules that steer traffic between tables are not read. |
| Is there an unexpected default route (a second gateway, a hijacked path)? | `routes` | Count the rows with `prefix_len` 0 per `family` and compare `gateway`, `interface` and `metric`. Windows and Linux give a metric; macOS has none and lists interface-scoped defaults (such as one per VPN tunnel) as ordinary rows. |
| Which networks go via which gateway? | `routes` | Non-default rows with a `gateway` are routed hops; a `gateway` of `-` is directly attached. `origin` says who installed the route, with a different vocabulary per OS (Caveat 5). |
| What are this device's addresses, MACs and link state? | `adapters`, `ip_addresses` | Per adapter. Tunnel-type adapters and loopback are skipped on Windows; see Caveat 2. |
| Which resolvers does it use? | `dns_servers` | Windows: per adapter. macOS: the dynamic store. Linux: only what `/etc/resolv.conf` lists, which on a host that runs a local resolver stub is the stub address, not the upstream servers. |
| Does it use a proxy? | `proxy` | Windows reports the agent account's settings (LocalSystem today), macOS reports HTTP and PAC only, Linux reports only variables the agent process inherited. A result of `none` is not a statement about any user's browser. |
| Who is on the local subnet? | `arp` | A cache of recently seen neighbours, not a scan. Linux shows IPv4 only; macOS rows have no interface name. |
| What names has the host resolved lately? | `dns_cache` | Windows and Linux only. An empty cache is not the same as "no lookups". |

### Diagrams

#### routes, by OS

The three OS legs end in the same decision. A table that was read but cut short or reduced (row cap, a malformed record, a multipath route shown by its first hop only) is `CONSTRAINED`; a table that could not be read, or whose dump failed before any route was decoded, is `UNAVAILABLE`; only a complete read is `OK`, and then zero rows is a genuinely empty table. An exception inside a leg is reported with return code 1.

#### Gateway meaning in `ip_addresses`

| OS | Where `gateway` comes from | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Windows | each adapter's own first gateway | a multi-homed host can show a different gateway on each adapter |
| macOS | one system default gateway, resolved once | the same value is repeated on every row |
| Linux | one main-table default gateway, resolved once | the same value is repeated on every row |

On macOS and Linux a host with several default routes still shows a single gateway here; `routes` is the action that shows all of them.
name: network_config

columns.description: Adapter's OS-reported display name (Windows friendly name; Linux/macOS kernel interface name). Values: free text.
columns.name: name

columns.description: Adapter's MAC address, colon-separated hex, or '-' when the leg could not resolve one (loopback, tunnel/utun interfaces).
columns.name: mac

columns.description: Link speed reported by the OS, in megabits per second; 0 when unknown, inactive, or not applicable (loopback/tunnel). Values: integer Mbps, 0 for unknown/inactive (Linux/macOS); Windows emits the unclamped TransmitLinkSpeed sentinel (18446744073709) instead of 0 when the adapter reports no known speed — see Caveats.
columns.name: speed_mbps

columns.description: Adapter link state. Windows/Linux report the OS's OPERATIONAL state (IfOperStatus / IFLA_OPERSTATE); macOS reports the ADMINISTRATIVE IFF_UP flag instead, so a cable-unplugged Mac NIC can read 'up' where Windows/Linux would read 'down'. Values: up, down (Windows, macOS); up, down, unknown (Linux, when the kernel omits IFLA_OPERSTATE).
columns.name: status

columns.description: Owning network interface name; always '-' on macOS, where the PF_ROUTE RTF_LLINFO dump carries no interface field. Values: interface name, or '-' (macOS, always).
columns.name: interface

columns.description: Neighbour's IPv4 or IPv6 address. Values: IPv4 or IPv6 literal.
columns.name: ip_address

columns.description: Neighbour's MAC address, colon-separated hex; '-' for a Windows entry with no resolved hardware address yet (incomplete). Linux drops all-zero-MAC rows rather than emitting '-'. Values: colon-separated hex, or '-' (Windows incomplete entries only).
columns.name: mac_address

columns.description: Static/dynamic/incomplete classification; always '-' on macOS, where the PF_ROUTE RTF_LLINFO dump carries no such distinction. Values: static, dynamic, incomplete (Windows only); static, dynamic (Linux); '-' (macOS, always).
columns.name: entry_type

columns.description: Resolved DNS name of the cached entry. Populated only on Windows — Linux emits opaque, unparsed resolvectl/systemd-resolve text under a different row shape, and macOS never populates this action at all. See Caveats. Values: free text (FQDN or reverse-lookup name).
columns.name: name

columns.description: DNS resource-record type of the cached entry, decoded from DnsGetCacheDataTable's wType. Populated only on Windows; an unrecognised wType value reports 'unknown'. Values: A, AAAA, CNAME, PTR, MX, SRV, unknown.
columns.name: record_type

columns.description: Always the literal 0 — the Windows leg does not decode a real time-to-live from DnsGetCacheDataTable's cache entry structure, so this is not a measured value.
columns.name: ttl

columns.description: Adapter owning this resolver on Windows; Linux and macOS report the system-wide resolver list under the literal value 'system' (resolv.conf and SCDynamicStore are not per-adapter). Values: adapter name (Windows), or the literal 'system' (Linux, macOS).
columns.name: adapter

columns.description: Configured DNS server address. Values: IPv4 or IPv6 literal.
columns.name: server

columns.description: Address family of the server value. Values: IPv4, IPv6.
columns.name: type

columns.description: Adapter name the address belongs to (same name as the adapters action's name field). Values: free text.
columns.name: adapter

columns.description: IPv4 or IPv6 unicast address assigned to the adapter; an IPv6 link-local zone suffix ('%ifname') is stripped on macOS. Values: IPv4 or IPv6 literal.
columns.name: address

columns.description: CIDR prefix length of the address's subnet. Values: integer, 0-32 (IPv4) or 0-128 (IPv6).
columns.name: prefix_length

columns.description: Default gateway address for this row. Windows resolves it per-adapter (FirstGatewayAddress); Linux/macOS resolve a single system-wide default gateway and repeat it on every row. Values: IPv4 literal, or '-' when none or unresolved.
columns.name: gateway

columns.description: Proxy mode. Windows and macOS emit a normalized type; Linux instead emits the literal environment-variable name it read (e.g. 'http_proxy', 'HTTPS_PROXY'), and can emit several proxy_type/proxy_address row pairs in one response if more than one variable is set — see Caveats. Values: none, http, pac, auto_detect (Windows); none, http, pac (macOS); none, or a literal *_proxy/ALL_PROXY variable name (Linux).
columns.name: proxy_type

columns.description: The proxy host:port (http), the PAC URL (pac), or the raw environment-variable value (Linux). Row is omitted entirely when proxy_type is none/auto_detect. Values: 'host:port', a URL, or a raw environment-variable value.
columns.example: not observed in the captured samples — omitted whenever proxy_type is none or auto_detect
columns.name: proxy_address

columns.description: Comma-separated proxy-exception/bypass list; the row is omitted entirely when the list is empty. Values: comma-separated free text.
columns.name: bypass

columns.description: Address family of the route. Values: ipv4, ipv6.
columns.name: family

columns.description: Destination network address; the default route is 0.0.0.0 or ::. Values: IPv4 or IPv6 literal.
columns.name: destination

columns.description: Destination prefix length in bits; 0 is the default route, 32 or 128 a host route. Values: 0-32 (ipv4), 0-128 (ipv6).
columns.name: prefix_len

columns.description: Next-hop address; '-' when the route is on-link (directly attached). Linux reports 'nhid:<n>' for a route that references an `ip nexthop` object whose gateway is not resolved, and the first nexthop's gateway for a multipath route. Values: IPv4 or IPv6 literal, 'nhid:<n>' (Linux only), or '-'.
columns.name: gateway

columns.description: Outgoing interface name; '-' when the interface index no longer resolves on Linux and macOS (or, for a Linux blackhole/unreachable/prohibit/throw route or an `ip nexthop` object route, when the route carries none); Windows renders `if<index>` when the alias lookup fails. Values: interface name, `if<index>` (Windows), or '-'.
columns.name: interface

columns.description: Route metric (the Linux priority; the Windows route metric, without the interface metric); '-' on macOS, which has no route metric. Values: decimal integer, or '-' (macOS, always).
columns.name: metric

columns.description: Linux routing table; '-' on Windows and macOS, which have a single table. Values: main, default, or a decimal table id (Linux); '-' (Windows, macOS).
columns.name: table

columns.description: Kind of route. Values: unicast, blackhole, unreachable, prohibit, throw, nat, xresolve, or type<N> for an unknown Linux rtm_type (Linux); unicast, blackhole, reject (macOS); unicast (Windows, always).
columns.name: route_type

columns.description: Who installed the route. Linux: the rtm_protocol name (kernel, boot, static, dhcp, ra, bgp, ospf, ...) or proto<N>. Windows: the NL_ROUTE_PROTOCOL name (local, netmgmt, dhcp, ...) or proto<N>. macOS: static when the kernel set RTF_STATIC (the kernel sets it on connected-interface routes too, which Linux calls kernel and Windows calls local), dynamic for RTF_DYNAMIC or RTF_MODIFIED, else other (the routing socket carries no protocol field). Values: protocol name, or proto<N>.
columns.name: origin

outputs_note:
Pipe-delimited rows via `write_output()`. `adapters`/`ip_addresses`/`dns_servers`/`arp`/`routes` each emit one
row per record under a single literal-prefix discriminator. `proxy` and `dns_cache` do **not** — see
their own notes below the field tables. `-` marks a value the leg could not resolve; it never means
zero, and it is not used as a "no rows" sentinel (a leg that finds nothing on `adapters`/
`ip_addresses`/`dns_servers`/`arp`/`routes` simply emits zero rows, which is itself a legitimate host state
distinguished from failure by the typed result status).



**`proxy` — not one row per record.** Each configured value is its own row: `proxy_type|<value>`,
`proxy_address|<value>` (omitted when there is no proxy), and `bypass|<value>` (omitted when the
list is empty). Windows/macOS emit at most one `proxy_type`/`proxy_address` pair; Linux can emit
several — see Caveats.

| Field | Type | Values | Available | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `proxy_type` | string | `none` `http` `pac` `auto_detect` (W); `none` `http` `pac` (M); `none`, or a literal `*_proxy`/`ALL_PROXY` variable name (L) | W, M, L | `auto_detect` |
| `proxy_address` | string | `host:port`, a PAC URL, or the raw env-var value (L) | W, M, L | not observed in the captured samples — omitted whenever `proxy_type` is `none`/`auto_detect` |
| `bypass` | string | comma-separated free text | W, M, L | `*.local,169.254/16` |

**`dns_cache` — no shared row shape across platforms.** Windows: `cache_entry|name|record_type|0|` (the literal `0` is a hardcoded placeholder, not a real TTL, and the trailing field is always empty; `do_dns_cache`). Linux (`resolvectl` path): `cache_entry|<raw resolvectl line>`, one opaque field, not split into name, type and TTL. Linux (`systemd-resolve` fallback): `dns_stats|<raw statistics line>`, a different discriminator entirely. Every platform also has sentinel rows: `dns_cache|empty` (Windows, zero entries), `dns_cache|not_available|<reason>` (Windows and Linux, tool missing or query failed), `dns_cache|unsupported|<reason>` (macOS, always). The three schema-mapped fields below apply to the Windows structured row only.

| Field | Type | Values | Available | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | string | free text (FQDN or reverse-lookup name) | W only | `windowsupdate.microsoft.com` |
| `record_type` | enum | `A` `AAAA` `CNAME` `PTR` `MX` `SRV` `unknown` | W only | `PTR` |
| `ttl` | int | literal `0` | W only | `0` |

privileges.grant: **None.** Every leg is a native Win32 read API; none requires elevation.
privileges.if_refused: no dedicated `PERMISSION_DENIED` path: a failed API call returns `rc=1` with an in-band error row (adapters, ip_addresses, dns_servers) or `GetIpNetTable2 failed (rc=N)` (arp); `routes` instead returns `rc=0` with `UNAVAILABLE`/`PARTIAL` `network_config:routes_table_unavailable`
privileges.measured: 2026-09-07 on bare metal as `SYSTEM`; `routes` 2026-10-03 on bare metal as `SYSTEM`

privileges.grant: **None.** `getifaddrs`, `ioctl(SIOCGIFMEDIA)`, routing-socket sysctl reads and `SCDynamicStore` reads all work unprivileged.
privileges.measured: 2026-09-07 as an unprivileged user (euid 501), below the agent's actual root runtime; `routes` 2026-10-03, also euid 501

privileges.grant: **None** for adapters, ip_addresses, dns_servers, proxy, arp and routes (native reads only). `dns_cache` runs `resolvectl` or `systemd-resolve` through the bounded direct-argv runner (no elevation needed, but the tool must be present).
privileges.measured: 2026-09-06 in a container as euid 0 (root), more privileged than the agent's real runtime; `routes` 2026-10-03, also euid 0 (an `RTM_GETROUTE` dump is an unprivileged read by design, but it was not measured below root)
privileges.runs_as: agent's own unprivileged account (`yuzu-agent` on the packaged unit)

result_status.when: clean read on any action/OS not listed below
Linux `adapters`, rtnetlink dump incomplete
macOS `adapters`/`ip_addresses`, `getifaddrs()` failed
Linux `ip_addresses`, link/addr/route dump incomplete, or a main-table default route in an unresolvable nexthop form
macOS `ip_addresses`, PF_ROUTE default-route sysctl truncated or failed
Linux `dns_servers`, `/etc/resolv.conf` unreadable
macOS `dns_servers`, SCDynamicStore session failed, or built without the SystemConfiguration framework
macOS `proxy`, `SCDynamicStoreCopyProxies` failed, or built without SystemConfiguration
Linux `dns_cache`, neither `resolvectl` nor `systemd-resolve` available/usable

Linux `dns_cache`, a `resolvectl`/`systemd-resolve` subprocess failure is forwarded via `yuzu::agent::forward_runner_failure` (its own CONSTRAINED/UNAVAILABLE classification; not independently verified here — see Caveats)
Linux `arp`, 20k-row cap hit, or `/proc/net/arp` unreadable/errored
macOS `arp`, PF_ROUTE ARP sysctl failed/truncated, or 20k-row cap hit
Windows `arp`, 20k-row cap hit
`routes` on any OS, the 20k-row cap was hit; the first 20,000 routes are reported, the table is longer

Linux `routes`, the RTM_GETROUTE dump did not complete (error, truncation, foreign-datagram flood, timeout, the kernel aborting it with an errno in the closing NLMSG_DONE, or the kernel flagging that the table changed during the read — NLM_F_DUMP_INTR, so rows may repeat or be missing); the rows decoded so far are reported
Linux `routes`, the dump failed before any route was decoded — no rows, never an empty table
Linux `routes`, at least one multipath route reported only its first nexthop, or an `ip nexthop` object route has no resolved gateway (reported as `nhid:<n>`)
macOS `routes`, the NET_RT_DUMP sysctl failed, or the table exceeded the 64 MiB read bound

macOS `routes`, a record header was malformed (the parse stops there, later routes are not reported) or a record had a non-contiguous netmask or an undecodable address (that route is skipped, the rest are reported)
Windows `routes`, `GetIpForwardTable2` failed
Windows `routes`, a route's destination could not be rendered and was left out
`routes` on any OS, an exception escaped a leg (e.g. an allocation failure); an `error|routes: internal error` row is written
Linux `dns_cache`, the `resolvectl`/`systemd-resolve` child process could not be spawned at all
Linux `dns_cache`, the runner's deadline elapsed while `resolvectl`/`systemd-resolve` was still running, and it was killed
Linux `dns_cache`, the `resolvectl`/`systemd-resolve` run was cancelled before it finished

where_the_data_goes: **Instruction result.** Rows travel over the agent's mTLS gRPC channel as the command response and land in the ResponseStore, queryable at `/api/responses/{id}`.

**Device page "Get live info".** `ip_addresses`, `arp` and `dns_cache` back three of the device page's live-snapshot cards (`device.live.netconfig` "Adapters & IP", `device.live.arp` "ARP", `device.live.dns_cache` "DNS cache"), dispatched through the shared "Get live info" chokepoint. This dispatch is deliberately untracked (no ExecutionTracker row, not in the executions drawer) because it fires one query per card on every click.

**Daily-sync device_ci source (ADR-0016).** `adapters` is one of the four plugin reads (`hardware`, `device_identity`, `os_info`, `network_config`) the `device_ci` daily-sync source invokes in process to build the device's configuration-item record; its MAC addresses are deduped and sorted, and the first becomes the record's primary MAC. A MAC address is device-identifying data, so this source is in the GDPR personal-data and behavioural-PII tier of the daily-sync routed concern. A failed `adapters` read aborts the whole sync cycle rather than syncing a partial record.
**Not consumed by** Echo, DEX or Prometheus metrics.

**Sensitivity.** `adapters` rows carry the host's own MAC addresses, and `arp` rows carry the MAC and IP address of every other device currently seen on the local subnet: device-identifying data by another route. `routes` rows carry the host's routing topology (internal networks, and the next-hop addresses and interface names of VPN and internal gateways), which is infrastructure detail rather than personal data. `ip_addresses` and `dns_servers` rows carry only this host's own address and resolver configuration. `dns_cache` entries can include hostnames of other devices the host has contacted (for example the names of phones or workstations on the LAN), which is potentially device-identifying. `proxy` rows carry network configuration only.

**Siblings:** `echo` has its own ARP collector that enumerates Windows ARP independently for the Echo capture surface; it is not a consumer of this plugin's `arp` action. `network_diag` covers listening ports and active connections, a distinct surface from this plugin's adapter, address, DNS and ARP inventory.

**MCP / REST.** Discover: `discover_plugins` (summary), then `yuzu://plugin-docs` (this page as data), then `discover_instructions` or `get_definition("device.network_config.arp")`. Run: `execute_instruction {definition_id, parameters}`. Read: `/api/responses/{id}`, or the device page's "Get live info" snapshot for `ip_addresses`, `arp` and `dns_cache`.
